analysis.one_liner: Gives people legal control over how companies collect, use, and sell their personal data.
analysis.headline: Senator Markey's online privacy bill, introduced in April 2019 with zero cosponsors, never received a committee hearing or floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Privacy Bill of Rights Act would require companies that collect personal information — names, browsing history, location, biometrics, and more — to get your explicit permission before collecting or sharing it, and to let you see, correct, or delete what they hold. It would ban companies from refusing service to people who decline to share data, ban discounts in exchange for data consent, prohibit selling biometric data like face and fingerprint scans, and stop advertisers from using personal data to discriminate in jobs, credit, housing, and insurance. The Federal Trade Commission, state attorneys general, and individuals could all enforce the rules, and companies could not force disputes into arbitration.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who uses the internet, apps, or any business that keeps records — consumers would gain the right to know what data companies hold, demand deletion, and refuse to trade privacy for service. People harmed by discriminatory ad targeting in employment, credit, housing, or insurance would gain a legal remedy, and victims of data breaches could sue instead of being forced into arbitration.

how_it_helps.text: Requires companies to get clear, opt-in approval before collecting, using, sharing, or selling personal information, and lets people withdraw that approval at any time [S2, S3].
Gives individuals the right to access, correct, delete, and take their data to another company, at no cost and without needing an account, and bans re-identifying supposedly anonymous data [S2, S3].
Prohibits 'take-it-or-leave-it' refusals of service to people who decline data collection, and bans discounts or price incentives offered in exchange for consent to surveillance [S3].

Bars companies from selling biometric data like face, fingerprint, and voice scans, and from processing personal data in ways that discriminate on race, sex, religion, disability, and other protected traits in jobs, credit, housing, insurance, and public accommodations [S2, S3].
Lets individuals sue for damages and attorney's fees, voids forced-arbitration clauses for privacy disputes, and allows FTC and state attorney general enforcement [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: Companies that collect and monetize personal data — tech platforms, advertising networks, and data brokers — would bear compliance costs, lose ad-targeting and data-sale revenue, and face new litigation exposure. Some costs would pass to consumers through prices and fewer 'free' ad-supported services.

drawbacks.text: The ban on financial incentives would prohibit common loyalty discounts and reduced-price services offered in exchange for data sharing, which some consumers value, and could raise the price of ad-supported 'free' services [S3].

The opt-in consent regime, data minimization limits, and mandatory privacy officers and audits would impose real compliance costs, falling hardest on small businesses rather than large platforms [S3].
A broad private right of action treating any violation as automatic legal injury, with punitive damages and no arbitration, could generate substantial litigation costs [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer gains — control over personal data, a right to deletion, and protection from discriminatory targeting — are broad and tangible. The costs are real but fall mostly on firms whose business model is data collection, with some pass-through to consumers in prices and friction. The main design risk is litigation-heavy enforcement, which the bill could have calibrated more tightly. On balance it is a strong consumer-protection bill with some overbreadth.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Edward Markey introduced the Privacy Bill of Rights Act on April 11, 2019 [S1].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, which is the last action recorded [S5].
The committee took no further action and the bill never reached the Senate floor before the Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that profit from collecting and selling personal data — data brokers, adtech networks, and large platforms — kept the status quo, facing no federal baseline privacy rights for consumers.

for.name: Edward J. Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Privacy Bill of Rights Act on April 11, 2019 and referred it to the Senate Commerce Committee.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after its referral; the bill died there.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no senator cosponsored the bill, so the record shows no measurable party split; the Senate Commerce Committee, then chaired by a Republican, simply never took it up.

industries.note: The bill targets brokers directly: it would require a public FTC list of every data broker, restrict what they can collect, and let consumers demand deletion. Their core business of selling profiles of people who are not their customers would shrink sharply [S3].
Opt-in consent, data minimization, bans on selling biometric data, and anti-discrimination rules would cut off much of the behavioral-targeting supply chain that ad networks monetize [S2, S3].

industries.industry: Large tech platforms and social media
industries.note: Platforms would face short-form privacy notices, opt-in consent, deletion rights, security audits, and individual lawsuits, and could no longer condition service or discounts on consent to data collection [S3].

Any business collecting personal information would take on compliance duties — notices, consent, deletion, security officers, audits — with costs hitting small firms hardest, while their customers gained the privacy rights the bill creates [S3].
